newsitem.title: USA: J.C. Penney says earnings hit by drug store buyout.
newsitem.headline: J.C. Penney says earnings hit by drug store buyout.

text.p: Major retail chains J.C. Penney Co. and Nordstrom Inc. Thursday reported sharp declines in fourth quarter results.
Plano, Texas-based J.C. Penney Co. said the steep drop in earnings were due to more than $200 million in charges to integrate its drug store business under the Eckerd Corp. name.

The retailer said earnings shrank to $94 million, or 36 cents a share, in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Jan. 25, from $326 million, or $1.31 a share, a year earlier. Sales jumped to $8.15 billion from $6.63 billion.
J.C. Penney said it took charges of $207 million in the quarter to integrate its drug stores acquisitions, a move that required the company to close some stores and write down some assets.
Last year, J.C. Penney bought the Eckerd drug store chain for $3.3 billion and also acquired another 190 Rite Aid stores in North Carolina and South Carolina for an undisclosed price.

The acquisition touched off concern at the Federal Trade Commission about concentration of ownership in the Carolinas. Under an agreement with the FTC, J.C. Penney worked out a plan to divest 161 drug stores in the states.
The federal agency was concerned that the company would have been in a position to raise prices for pharmarcy services for health insurance companies and other third-party purchasers.
Prior to acquiring Eckerd's 1,724 drug stores in 13 states, J.C. Penney owned more than 1,000 drug stores in 17 states through its Pittsburgh-based Thift Drug subsidiary.

For the fiscal 1996 year, the company reported earnings of $565 million, or $2.25 a share, on sales of $22.65 billion. That was down from year-earlier profits of $838 million, or $3.33 a share, on sales of $20.56 billion.
J.C. Penney's stock closed down 12.5 cents at $47.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Seattle-based Nordstrom said weak holiday sales, higher inventories than planned, higher markdowns and an increase in inventory "shrinkage" contributed to a decline in fourth quarter net income.

Dan Nordstrom, a co-president of the upscale department store chain, said the impact of a merchandise reorganization in women's apparel was mostly behind the company but probably would have "some lingering effects."
"We are pleased with customer response to our stores in promising new markets but disappointed with lower net income," he said in the company's earnings statement.

Nordstrom reported fourth quarter net income of $42.8 million, or 53 cents a share -- far below the Wall Street consensus figure of 64 cents a share -- compared with a year earlier's $54.1 million, or 67 cents a share.
Sales were $1.32 billion, up from $1.24 billion.

While comparable-store sales, or sales from stores open at least a year, rose 5.4 percent in January, they fell 3.8 percent in the crucial month of December and fell 1.3 percent for the quarter. For the year comparable-store sales rose 0.6 percent.
Nordstrom said parts of its holiday merchandising strategy were not executed as well as planned, such as the assortment of gift items.
Nordstrom earned $147.5 million, or $1.82 a share, in all of 1996, down from $165.1 million, or $2.02 a share, in 1995. Sales rose to $4.45 billion from $4.11 billion in 1995.
Nordstrom stock closed up 25 cents at $36 on Nasdaq.
